title: The Story of the Bicycle
source: Original passage written for this demonstration (no ReadWorks content)
content:
Today, millions of people around the world ride bicycles to school, to work, and for fun. It is hard to imagine a time without them. But the bicycle took more than seventy years, and many strange experiments, to become the machine we know.

The first ancestor of the bicycle appeared in 1817. A German inventor named Karl von Drais built a wooden machine with two wheels, a seat, and a steering handle. It had no pedals. To make it move, the rider pushed along the ground with both feet, like a child on a scooter. People called it the running machine. It was fun to ride on smooth roads, but it was slow, and many people thought it was only a toy.

In the 1860s, French inventors added pedals to the front wheel. These machines were called velocipedes. They were heavy and hard on the body, and because their wooden wheels had iron rims, they shook the rider on every bump. People nicknamed them boneshakers.

Then came the high wheelers, which were popular in the 1870s. To make the bicycle go faster, makers built the front wheel very large. Every turn of the pedals pushed the bicycle farther. Riders sat high above the ground, with a tiny wheel behind them. The high wheeler looked dramatic, but it was dangerous. If the front wheel hit a stone, the rider could be thrown over the handlebars. Falls were common, and they were serious.

The big change came in 1885. An English inventor named John Kemp Starley built a bicycle with two wheels of nearly the same size. A chain connected the pedals to the back wheel, so the rider could sit low, close to the ground. This design was safer, easier to learn, and faster than the high wheeler. It was called the safety bicycle, and it looks very much like the bicycles we ride today.

A few years later, in 1888, a Scottish veterinarian named John Boyd Dunlop made another improvement. He wanted his young son to have a smoother ride on a tricycle, so he wrapped rubber tubes around the wheels and filled them with air. The air cushion absorbed the bumps. Soon, almost every bicycle had air-filled tires.

By the 1890s, bicycles were everywhere. Many people could afford them, and they gave ordinary families a new kind of freedom. A worker could travel farther to a job. A young person could visit friends in the next town. Women in particular found that the bicycle gave them independence, and bicycle clubs were soon formed across Europe and America.

Bicycles even helped to start the age of flight. Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio. The skills they learned about balance, light materials, and moving parts helped them build the first successful airplane.

Today bicycles are still changing. Some have electric motors that help riders climb hills. Others are built from light materials such as carbon fiber. Cities are building bike lanes, because bicycles are quiet and clean and good for people's health.

The long story of the bicycle shows how a simple idea can improve over time. Each inventor looked at the problems of the last machine and tried to solve them. The result is one of the most useful inventions in history, and it began with a wooden running machine and a very brave rider.
